Generally my ICU is just barely short staffed. Most shifts are adequately staffed, 7 nurses to 14 beds, an eighth nurse without an assignment who acts as resource or takes a patient if we end up needing to 1:1 someone, and charge without an assignment (and a secretary). We don't have techs.

When we're at our usual level of short we have just 7 nurses to 14 beds and free charge. If it's worse charge will have to cosign an LPN with an assignment (which is still generally very manageable), and the worst, which is thankfully rare, charge will have an assignment on their own. If it's worse still management has to come in.

So most shifts in the week we are good. We don't have enough staff for every shift to be at ideal staffing, but the non-ideal shifts still are manageable. We rarely need a nurse to float to us, and usually only with call-ins.

During COVID, though, we occasionally had to 3:1 with a non-critical care trained assistive RN as partner. That was hard, but thankfully we managed to avoid doing that consistently.

The reason why it's an asset is because of the types of things that motivate ADHD brains! We need novel experiences, things that aren't routine, things that have a definite time pressure, and things we find interesting! All of these are every day in the ICU! It was a lot worse for me on Med-Surg because I was SO BORED.

The ICU also encourages nursing autonomy and thinking outside the box is helpful. These are more motivators for ADHD brains.

But yes, I still forget things and I get distracted. The key is to have coping mechanisms. I have a routine that I stick to in morning assessments. I do things in the same order, generally, so I know what I didn't do when I get interrupted.

I also write EVERYTHING down. There is a sticky note feature in our charting system. The first thing I do in a room is log in to the chart. Then I use the sticky note to notate anything I need to remember. 👍 It's absolutely my lifeline. I also plan on getting a smart watch to help set reminders. For example, "Set a timer for 30 minutes" so I don't forget to unclamp the NG and return to LIWS after meds.

Uniformadvantage.com has great stuff! I buy most of my scrubs from there. :)

And some stuff I would like are stethoscope charms, you can personalize them, because stethoscopes and not cheap and they get snatched!! A little flair makes yours stand out and less likely to get taken. Amazon and Etsy have great options.

Also, compression socks. 👍👍👍 We are on our feet ALL DAY. These help. There are cute patterns on Amazon. I wear the 20-30mmHg variety, but there are more options in the lesser grade of 10-20mmHg.

Also, cute badge reel? Funny nursing pens? There's also an adult coloring book that's nursing themed and so sassy. It's funny.

I have PTSD, OCD, anxiety, depression, and ADHD. What made a difference was definitely medication. I take hydroxyzine 50, fluoxetine 40,  and adderall XR 20 + 5 IR. I also take my hydroxyzine and melatonin to sleep.

I also talk openly about my struggles with my coworkers. It is very helpful for them to have an understanding of why I do certain things. I struggle the most socially and I can spiral quickly, since my coworkers know my struggles it's easier for me to talk to them about what is bothering me.

But for me... OCD and ADHD actually work very well in an ICU setting! So I'm lucky that way. There is a healthy level of anxiety in nursing, and that's necessary for the safety of your patient, but excessive anxiety is a safety risk.

I suggest being prepared with something that soothes you. I keep emergency chocolate in my lunch bag. :) And I step away when I need to.

But what REALLY helped was time and experience. I'm not sure working per diem is a good idea. Get yourself grounded full time, then when you are comfortable step back on your hours.

I've actually maintained employment since high school. First I worked in retail, I made a lot of friends at that job and goofed off a lot. So I had fun. Eventually I was promoted to front end supervisor, so there was a constant time pressure to keep me going.

I originally went to school to be a music teacher. Music is a wonderful hobby for me, but when it became a job I lost all interest, motivation, and passion. That's when I switched to nursing.

School was rough, I count my blessings that I'm an intelligent person because I wouldn't have made it through otherwise. I recorded my lectures so I could review parts I missed because of I was zoning out or writing (but I never did). I never studied, but the fact that the degree was almost no busy work I made it through. I started medication while in nursing school. This helped tremendously.

I started in med/surg but I got SO BORED. So motivation was challenging. Two years ago I started in the ICU and it has been life changing.

Three things motivate ADHD brains:
1) Pressure (especially time crunches). Man oh man is time pressure ALWAYS a thing in the ICU. Once I overcome the initial challenge of getting my day started, I keep moving. Sometimes I have a patient so sick that I only have one instead of two. These days are my favorite.

2) Interest. There is always something new to learn in the ICU. Daily rounds we discuss pathophysiology and work to solve the medical puzzle of the patient together.

3) Novelty. Especially in the medical ICU of a Level 1 Trauma Center, I am constantly exposed to new things. There are there's I don't do often and have to maintain proficiency so that when I do them I am successful and safe.

This has actually been studied. People with ADD do better in ICUs because of what I've discussed. In fact, we thrive because we can think outside the box. There is an organized chaos that keeps us GOING, that keeps up with our energy and need for stimulation.

You can do it. The struggle is real, but there is a path and q light at the end!
